summary.title: 500 Lines or Less: DBDB (Dog Bed Database)
summary.one_liner: Learn how a small Python key/value database works internally, covering immutable binary trees, copy-on-write updates, file locking, and atomic, durable commits.
takeaways: How DBDB separates the physical storage layer, logical tree layer, and public dictionary-style API.
Why an immutable binary tree lets updates build a new root that shares unchanged subtrees, making commits atomic.
How commits flush data to disk before atomically writing the root address, giving durability.
Why locking, dirty reads, and lack of compaction or isolation are trade-offs, and how B+ trees would improve I/O.
summary.summary: The author walks through DBDB, a small Python key/value store that persists to disk and avoids loading all data into RAM. The chapter tours the project's modules from the user-facing tool and interface down to the physical storage layer, then traces a get and a set-plus-commit through the code. It explains how immutable binary tree nodes enable copy-on-write updates, how a lockfile serializes writers, and how flushing data before atomically updating the root address provides atomicity and durability. It closes with limitations (no isolation, no compaction) and exercises on B+ trees and compaction.
